utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow me, follow what I'm saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a chair. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Anna Richterova, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Richterova. Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, with David Cunningham and Sasa Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I Thank you, and good morning to you too. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have three very brief preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The first one is we are withdrawing the Sipovo motion for Rule 92 bis witnesses. There was only one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me get the document, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. This motion was filed on 8th of May, 2003, and we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've taken note of that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We advised Mr. Ackerman yesterday. The other thing is we -- the Prosecution would like to request conference 65 ter, if it is possible today after the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Purpose of the conference that you are requesting?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is about the Scheduling Order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You can say what you need to say here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on, the microphone. You can say what you need to say here, Madam Richterova. The main reason being that today we need to be out of this courtroom by a quarter to 2.00, if not before. So there is absolutely no way we can have a 65 ter meeting today. That's for sure. Tomorrow I think we are pretty much in the same position, because probably I'm going to have Initial Appearance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We would like to request this conference in chambers, if it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the purpose? What is your specific request?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I was just instructed by Ms. Korner to request this conference, and I would be provided later with more information with respect to this conference. I'm not at this moment ready to talk about this. But also because we are three witnesses scheduled for today, so it was the reason, just ask for this conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want details, because the whole concept of the Rule 65 ter meetings outside and post the pre-trial stage is very much limited. So in order to grant a 65 ter meeting, I must know precisely what is the purpose of the meeting and -- because if the same things can be achieved or discussed in open session, I will have them discussed in open session, particularly knowing what has happened in the past when I granted you 65 ter meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I will raise this issue tomorrow and I will be more specific, if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the last thing is with respect to the following witness, not the one who will be called by Ms. Sutherland, but BT71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This witness was granted protective measures, facial and voice distortion; however, in my opinion, in the Prosecution's opinion, the nature of her testimony and the unique situation, I think that it is necessary that she testifies in closed session, like other witnesses who will talk about the -- can we go to the private session for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's better if we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Before we bring in the witness, Mr. Ackerman, please, Mr. Cunningham: Celinac municipality. You filed an objection to the OTP exhibits on the 5th of June. We dealt with Exhibits P1986, 1991 and 1992 already, in the course of the hearing of the 5th of June, and we decided to admit those three documents. However, you had also objected to the following proposed exhibits: P1987, P107, P110, and P1990. The argument that you bring forward, Mr. Ackerman, is that these are newspaper articles; therefore, they constitute hearsay and unreliable evidence or proof that cannot be tested through cross-examination. You brought up the same argument that you went into during the oral hearing on the 5th or I don't remember exactly when. Then you also argued with regard to P1987 that the author is unknown. And you do concede inter alia that P107 and P110 have already been admitted into evidence. I put it to you that with regard to 107 and 110, there is nothing to say at the present moment, at the present time, because they have already been admitted. And with regard to the other two, that perhaps we could, taking account of your objection which was dealt with previously, as I said, we could hand down our decision orally here and now. So, Ms. Sutherland, Madam Richterova, the documents P1987 and P1990 are being admitted in evidence, with the usual caveat that their probative value will be assessed at a later point in time when the Trial Chamber comes to that exercise. In the meantime, they are being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a few very brief matters. With regard to what you just talked about, I included the two exhibits that had already been admitted because it's my understanding that basically anything the Prosecution is offering is being admitted, at least provisionally, and later on that it can be reconsidered. And so what I was basically asking for was reconsideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I took it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based upon that new incomprehensible submission that I have made. With regard to the 92 bis responses, the Prosecutor has withdrawn Sipovo, Bosanska Krupa and Bosanski Novi will be filed this afternoon. It's going to take us another day or two with Kotor Varos or maybe even three, but we'll have it in this week. With regard to the Prosecution's request for a 65 ter conference, I may not be here in the morning when they renew that request, so I just want it very clear on the record that we are not joining in that request. We would appear, if you decide to have such a hearing, of course, but we're not joining the Prosecution in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my cross-examination of this upcoming witness is not going to last more than 30 or 45 minutes, and at the conclusion of that period of time I'd ask permission to depart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there will be any objection to that. So Witness -- does he enjoy any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. So Usher, could you please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to deliver some documents to the translation booth, so I'll just be a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start the witness, may we adjourn the witness at 1.30 this afternoon, whichever witness that we are dealing with then, so that I may advise the Chamber of the reasons that we -- the Prosecution is requesting that Ms. Richterova and myself attend in chambers with Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Cunningham? But basically, it deals with the importance of the witnesses that are coming up and the burden that that is going to be placing on Mr. Ackerman's health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Ms. Sutherland, you can file it in writing straight away, and without at any moment pretending to speak for Mr. Ackerman, who can speak for himself, and then we'll take everything into consideration after having heard Mr. Ackerman, and we will decide accordingly. But I am telling you that it will not be very easy to convince me to grant a 65 ter meeting. Would the witness please stand up. Good morning to you, sir, and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to give evidence very shortly. Before you do so, our Rules require that you enter a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that you have just been handed. Please read that aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please take a chair. Let me try and explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. You gave -- you're here not to give a full testimony, because statements that you have made before are being taken into consideration and brought into the body of evidence of this -- in this case. You are here to be cross-examined by the Defence counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin, Mr. Ackerman, and your obligation is to answer each and every question that is put to you in as full and as truthful a manner as possible. If there is any question that you shouldn't answer, we will stop you from answering it. We will protect you. But otherwise, unless we tell you not to answer a question, please try to answer the question as fully as you can. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was wanting to ask the witness a few preliminary questions before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a question about that. If instead of being brought for cross-examination, this witness is now being brought as a viva voce witness, then isn't it appropriate to withdraw the Rule 92 bis request? The Rule provides that the witness may be brought for cross-examination and now the Prosecution wants to conduct direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have done it before, I mean provided these are most of the time routine questions more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can ask him where he was born and things like that. It am just -- I just am curious about it. That's all. I have no major objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have allowed it in the past, provided it was limited to not the substance but --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to take the witness through, since his statements are being tendered as evidence, I want to -- he has made three corrections to his ICTY statement which I wanted to correct on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's how we have done it in the past, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then there is one other matter that I wish to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the corrections are in writing, and I assume Your Honours have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have them, but they are not being tendered in evidence; no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would have no objection to them being tendered into evidence. It will save us a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Do proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if I see that you are going beyond the -- what is proper, then I will stop you. But for the time being, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Vahid Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were born on the 10th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That you don't need to. Go straight -- because that is included in the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, since coming to the Tribunal you've had an opportunity to review the statements that you've made, and you made three corrections to your statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 9th of April, 2000, it states that you have six brothers and one sister. In fact, you have five brothers and one sister; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your brother Mujo, who was married to Halima, who died on the 1st of August, 1992; Ramadan; Raif; Dzevad, who was married to Djevida, who was wounded on the 1st of August, 1992; and Naim. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also in that statement, you stated that the person in charge of the Territorial Defence was Gojko Djuric.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He was in charge of the Territorial Defence in Popovac village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said, please. Could you repeat your answer, your reply.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence, Sahinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say he was the commander of the Territorial Defence -- Sahinovic --

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Gojko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also stated in your statement that on the 1st of August, 1992, at 1700 hours, the first killing took place in Basici, and in fact this should read on the 31st of July, 1992, at 1900 hours, the first killings took place in Basici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the statements of this witness taken on the 9th of April, 2000 and the 21st of February, 2003 as Exhibit P1980.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. The one of 9th April is P --?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: P1980. And there's another statement, a very short statement correcting the statement of the 9th of April, 2000, dated the 21st of February, 2003. I don't know whether you want them to be contained within the one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it could be within the same exhibit number. So it will be .1 and .2?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that's all right with you. I mean, it's up to you. And the statement of the 26th and 27th -- no, no. Sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're only seeking to tender the statements provided to the Office of the Prosecutor. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2005.7, and it is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: These are power -- some houses in the village of Basici. You can see the Mujkanovic house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Taking the pointer and pointing on the machine to your right --

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is Ljubo Mujkanovic's house, that one there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript -- the translation -- the interpretation we got was Ljubo's house. Did you say Ejub's house?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Ejub.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're pointing to the house up on the hill in the background of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that photograph. Sir, in your statement, you go into detail about the killing of Ejub Mujkanovic and Halima Mujkanovic and the wounding of Ismeta and Dzevida Mujkanovic. And as His Honour informed you when you first began your testimony that these statements are in evidence now and will be taken into consideration. I just want to ask you one matter. In relation to your brother Mujo, before he left the municipality of Celinac, did he have to obtain or did he obtain a death certificate for his wife Halima?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who provided the death certificate for his wife?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody got it for him. These documents were received only after the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your brother Mujo speak to anyone in the municipal authorities about obtaining a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court the circumstances about him attending at the municipal authority building.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: He went to the municipal hall to seek the death certificate and report the death of his wife, who was killed, and they said they couldn't do it. They could not say that she had been killed, that he had to sign a statement that she had died of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why did they say they couldn't do it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: That I don't know. I suppose because they were saying that there were no murders and the like in the municipality of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your brother tell you that that's what they said?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the death certificate amended at any point?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was issued the death certificate of the identification of the dead bodies in 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please raise your voice. The interpreters are having trouble hearing you. Was your brother's wife's body exhumed in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was the death certificate then amended?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. That is, the first time he was issued with a death certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what was the cause of death on the death certificate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: She had died violently. That is what the book said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman. And you may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you first about this last issue that the Prosecutor has been talking to you about, and that is the issuance of this death certificate. Okay? Now, I suspect that if you went to the municipality, in any municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina today, and informed them that your wife had been murdered and that she would like a death certificate to show that, they would refuse to issue it to you without proof that she had been murdered. Don't you suspect that's the case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there was proof, because at that time the police reserve force normally went out to the sites of murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that the circumstances of her death were available at that time, but as I understand it, they were not made available to the municipal authorities, those circumstances, other than simply your brother saying that he would like them to issue a death certificate showing that she had been killed. And they were only willing to issue a death certificate basically showing that she was dead, if he would certify that she was dead. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. It could be confirmed by the civilian authorities, which had come out to conduct the on-site investigation, and they refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it could have been, but nobody asked them to. As I understand it, your brother just went there and said: I want this death certificate, and I want it to show that she was killed. And they said: Not without further information. And as I understand it, he made no effort to get an official report from the police or anyone else to prove to them the circumstances of her death. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, nobody believed anything that a Bosniak might have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that's your position, but you didn't answer my question. As I understand it, your brother made no effort to get an official report from the police or any other authority to prove the circumstances of his wife's death, but simply asked that the death certificate be issued upon his word alone.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: But they didn't give it to him. The police didn't give him its report. Because the civilian authorities in the municipality did not come, or any physician, to establish death. And it is a common fact that whenever somebody dies, there must be a doctor's opinion and his finding, but that didn't happen. They wouldn't allow any physician come near our dead or wounded or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So now what you've just told us is that a death certificate could not be issued showing the cause of death unless that death certificate was signed by a physician who had made that determination; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the year 1990, you told us in your report that you were working illegally in Graz in Austria; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was it that was illegal about your working there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How were you able to actually work there if it was illegal, if you didn't have any papers? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I went to Austria, found a job, and I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The person who hired you, didn't they ask for your papers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When 1991 came around, did you get involved in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement, which has been admitted in evidence in this case, you say -- you said this at one point: "As soon as the war in Croatia started, local Serbs volunteered to fight." When you said in your statement "local Serbs," who are you including in that? Is that just the village of Basici or the Celinac municipality, or who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were those, the neighbours in the village of Kablovi, and people from the municipality of Celinac too who went to report for service of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you went on to say that Muslims did not respond to the mobilisation, and again, you're referring to the Celinac municipality, Muslims in the Celinac municipality?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's the village of Basici I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In that instance, then, you're limiting that to the village of Basici, the Muslims of Basici did not respond; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you say this: "The president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, instructed all Muslims not to go fight in Croatia." How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Through mass media, through media of mass information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That could be radio, television, or newspaper. Do you remember which?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Through the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "news," do you mean radio?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: TV news.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you remember about when it was that you learned that through the TV news?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why was it that the Muslims of Basici decided to obey what Mr. Izetbegovic had instructed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic called upon all -- the whole population of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to respond to mobilisation. How people -- what people understood that to mean, I don't know. It varied from one man to another. But this is the way I understood it, and I did not respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware that some Muslims responded to the mobilisation call in spite of what Izetbegovic said?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And don't you know that significant numbers of Muslims in the Celinac municipality in fact responded to the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us that Serbs were selling weapons to Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, many Muslims, those are your words, many Muslims bought weapons from Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, that Muslims were buying weapons from Serbs and then reselling them to other Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You bought a Zastava 7.62, for which you paid 1.200 Deutschmarks, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber what a Zastava 7.62 is. Describe it to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a pistol, calibre 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it automatic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: A pistol cannot be semi-automatic. Everybody knows that. We all know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't have to cock it every time you wanted to fire it, did you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I never fired from it. It was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please repeat your last reply. You started by saying: "I never fired from it." And then you said something else which the interpreters didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I never fired from it, that I bought it as a new weapon, and it was seized from me as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, if I suggested to you that probably the vast majority of pistols are semi-automatic, would you disagree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree, because now I have a weapon with a licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is it a pistol?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it it's not a Zastava.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you purchased this Zastava, did you buy ammunition for it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How much?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Two clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many bullets per clip?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Eight bullets per clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you had 16 rounds of ammunition and this pistol?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For that, you paid 1.200 Deutschmarks. That's a pretty high price, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the price.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was illegal for you to own that weapon, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any concern that the Serb who sold it to you was just going to turn you in for having an illegal weapon?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that because he was a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he didn't know you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was it that this transaction happened? It didn't happen in Basici, I take it.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did it happen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: In Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a time, then, didn't there, where there was a call for the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a few Muslims from your village, Basici, in fact did surrender their weapons to the Crisis Staff in Popovac?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you told us five weapons were surrendered.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you said that those of you who had illegal weapons did not surrender them; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said that those were kept by you for your protection?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the middle of June, four policemen came to your house who knew that you had this Zastava, and asked that you turn it in?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: So they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You asked them to come into your house so you could give them the weapon, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what they told you was they couldn't do that, they didn't have the warrants necessary to permit them to enter your house; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because they couldn't come in your house, they asked you to bring the weapon out?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you brought out the weapon, plus the two clips of bullets, and turned those over to the police?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You gave them all of the ammunition that you had, plus the weapon, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... four police on that occasion was very correct, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then three days later, one of those police officers came to your house and asked you and the other persons who had turned in weapons to report to Crisis Staff headquarters in Popovac the next morning; right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And seven of you went there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the commander of the reserve police asked if you were the owners of the weapons that had been turned in?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And five of you admitted that you were, and two of you denied it, and the ones who denied it were set free?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the people that was set free said the weapon was licensed, and you say the other lied and said it was not his weapon.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those of you who admitted it were detained in the cellar of that building for a short time and you were not mistreated or beaten at all?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were then taken to Celinac, where you spent one night at the police station there. You were questioned but not beaten?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the next morning you were taken before a misdemeanour judge who sentenced you to 25 days in prison for possession of an illegal weapon?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that prison sentence was served at the Tunjice prison in Banja Luka, for a period of 25 days, during which time you were not mistreated; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And after you had served that sentence, you received a document, written permission to return to Basici; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you got back to Basici, Basici was under blockade. You showed your papers to a soldier, a Serb soldier, upon arrival --

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that soldier walked you through the checkpoints so that you could safely return to your village, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about the killings that you -- just very briefly about the killings that you described that occurred in Basici, and you made a correction today that the first of those was on 31 July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All the killings that you have described that occurred in the village of Basici were at the hands of the Sugic brothers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Sugic brothers were from the neighbouring village of Popovac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked about three people being killed in the Basici village.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there came a time when you wanted to bury these three people at the Muslim cemetery but you were unable to go there, so you, along with another person, went to Gojko Djuric and asked him to allow you to do the burial at the Muslim cemetery; right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you understand English; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We just happen to have very efficient interpreters, Mr. Ackerman, because actually you're going at quite a speed, both of you, and I was wondering. But they are short questions and short answers, so the ideal situation. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric told you at that point that it would be too dangerous for you to go there because there were extremist Serbs in the area who might shoot you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I get the impression from hearing that and reading that that the TO was involved in the process of trying to protect you from these extreme Serb elements. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, on the 6th of August, just right around the time that you were trying to do these burials, Djuric came to you and said that the situation had gotten to the point that he could no longer guarantee your safety, and for your safety, you should leave that area. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so you did leave, and after a little bit of travelling around, you wound up at Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's in the Banja Luka municipality, I believe. You stayed there until July -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You stayed there until July 1993, and then you went to Travnik, which was Muslim-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say that in 1985, 1986, that you were working on a construction site that was being supervised by Radoslav Brdjanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was that construction site?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in Tunjice, at the brickworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever work with Mr. Brdjanin in Zagreb, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any of your brothers did? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You told the Prosecutor that you didn't ever see Mr. Brdjanin during the year 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did not, you did not see him during 1992 or you didn't tell the Prosecutors that you did not see Mr. Brdjanin during 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say you didn't see him, that would include seeing him on television, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't see him on television either, did you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a person who lived in Celinac in 1992 by the name of Sutka Spahic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Supko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that person?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at an exhibit. Maybe this will help refresh your memory. It's been marked as DB 143. I want you to see DB 143B, which is the Serbian version. Now, what you have before you, sir, is a decision from the Executive Board of the Celinac municipality, and it appoints a graduate engineer of architecture by the name of Sutka Spahic, to a position in the Celinac municipality. And it appears to be signed by Radoslav Brdjanin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see the name Spahic, Sutka in that document. Does that --

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does that now remind you of who that person was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I would recognise them from seeing them around, but I didn't have any direct contacts with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that the president of the municipality was named Spahic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not this person was his wife?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you know by the name that this person was a Bosniak, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the document shows Mr. Brdjanin appointing a Muslim to a position on the 11th of May of 1992, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for your time, and I hope you have a good trip home. We appreciate your coming. Thank you for being so brief and so forth in answering my questions. It's helped us a great deal, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Sutherland, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on. Ms. Sutherland, is there re-examination, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked whether Gojko Djuric and the TO were trying to protect the Muslim population and you said that that wasn't correct.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Because they are the ones who did all of that. A part of their Territorial Defence did what they did to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you say what they did to us, are you referring to the killings and the wounding of people in your villages?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement, and you briefly referred to it in your cross-examination, you said that the villages of Basici and Mehovci were barricaded in.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was responsible for doing this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I believe that you said that the village was barricaded from sometime in May until you were expelled in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you weren't allowed to leave your villages at all during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. There are no questions from the Bench, which basically means, sir, that your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Tribunal and particularly on behalf of Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself, who are presiding over this trial, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence, even if this involved only a few minutes of evidence. But we do appreciate your effort and your availability. I can assure you that on behalf -- that everyone here wishes you a safe journey back home. Before you leave this courtroom, before you're escorted out, may I assure you that you will receive all the assistance you require to help you return home as quickly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the witness room in this courtroom always on this side? Is there another one on the other side or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There are two waiting rooms, so the next witness will be in that other room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do we know need to close down the curtains, Usher? Mr. Ackerman, shall we see you tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour. Mr. Cunningham and I are discussing how we're going to proceed for the rest of the week. I may not be here tomorrow. We'll see. But thank you, Your Honour. May I depart now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is the usher. He went with the witness, yes. If we can gain time or not waste time. Yes, usher. We need to bring the curtains down. Please help the registrar. So the next witness is 7.114; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, 7.114, and the pseudonym is BT71.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. We have voice and facial distortion for this witness, so I don't know whether the technicians are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether they need time to put the voice distortion in place. Because probably they do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the technical installation of the voice distortion would take approximately ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have no option but -- if there is any business that we can deal with in these ten minutes, we can do it, but otherwise I think we'll just suspend the sitting for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- earlier break and start quarter to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask the cooperation of everyone, in order not to waste time, and also because we may need to leave a little bit earlier than usual, if we could reduce the break to 20 minutes. The interpreters and the technicians in particular. Is that agreeable to you, Mr. Cunningham and Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't have an objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And then if there is a problem, then obviously you'll let us know. So it's 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, madam, and welcome to this Tribunal. Let me explain to you a few things before you start giving evidence. You have asked for certain protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are the microphones of the witness switched on? Thank you. You have asked, first of all, that you will not be referred to by your name, and indeed we have granted that. You will be referred to by a number, a pseudonym. You are BT--?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: BT71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: BT71, and that's how you will be known inside this Tribunal for the purposes of this case. You also asked for voice distortion, which basically means that people outside this courtroom will not be able to hear your real voice, but they will hear a travesty of it, a completely changed, distorted voice, which is not your own. So as a result, no one should be in a position to recognise you, to identify who is giving evidence here, because your voice, as such, will be changed, distorted. You also asked for face distortion, visual distortion, and this has also been granted. If you look at your monitor now on video mode, you will see how anyone else outside this courtroom will be seeing you. So no one will be able to see your face, because of the squares, cubes, that you see on your screen. That we call visual distortion, and that is by way of a protective measure to hide further your identity. Now, the Prosecution this morning asked us to grant that your testimony be given in closed session, which basically means that it will be completely private, no one will have access to it outside these four walls, outside these four walls. The Defence have agreed, first of all, that you do not need to go through the details that you describe in your statement regarding the alleged sexual assault. The Prosecution is going to be presenting your statement, which the three of us have already read, in any case, and know the contents of, and that will spare you having to tell us the sad part of the story again and again. This is to spare you. If instead you prefer to say it again, we will give you every opportunity. I don't want you to consider this as a means to shut your mouth at all. I mean, I'm just trying to spare you. I have heard cases like this before, and I know what a woman who has gone through such events as you describe in your statement go through again in giving evidence, and I'm trying to avoid this -- spare you having to do this. I am pleased that Mr. Cunningham, appearing for Mr. Brdjanin here, the accused in this trial, has agreed to this, and therefore there will not be any need for that. However, you will be asked, of course, other questions about other matters. There are certain instances arising from your statement which, if given in an open session, even though we are hiding your face, your voice, et cetera, will reveal your identity, and therefore we will in due course, as you proceed in your testimony, there will be moments when we will go into closed session, but not for the entire sitting. There may be instances where we can be in open session. There may be instances in which we can be in private session, which is more or less very similar to closed, but we will try to protect your identity as much as we can, and at the same time, safeguard one of the principles which surrounds and which govern such trials, namely, the publicity, that the proceedings ought to be as public as possible. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you agree to give testimony under these conditions? So the next thing that you need to do is stand up. You are going to be given the text of a solemn declaration. (Redacted) (Redacted)--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (Redacted). But this is the equivalent of an oath. In other words, you will be making a solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, you need to turn off your ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to raise your voice a little bit, because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that the microphone is functioning properly. Did the interpreters hear her voice or not? No, I don't even hear interpreters myself. Can the interpreters hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear you, Your Honour, but we cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't hear the witness. So we have a problem. Can the witness try to speak again into the microphone, please. Is it switched on, usher? Make sure that it is switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. They have heard you now. Please take a chair and relax. And last thing I want to say before we start is that as soon as the witness stops speaking, talking, or while she is talking, sorry, while she is talking, all other microphones must be switched off. That's very important. All right? I'll be keeping an open eye. So madam, you are now going to be asked a few questions by Madam Richterova, and after that you will be cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham. Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I will show you a piece of paper on which you will see your name. Please just confirm, yes or no, whether it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please show it to Mr. Cunningham and to ourselves. Thank you. And that is being tendered and received as Exhibit number P19 --?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This will be P2114, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2114, under seal. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, I do not want you now to mention any names, and just describe the events as I am going to ask you. When was your husband released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: On the 16th of November -- 16th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he tell you what happened to him while he was in police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please describe what he told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: One day he was in the lavatory, naked. He was beaten and forced to sing some songs. And then they took him to an office, and he spent five days sitting on a chair. And they kept beating him, and he showed me how on his thigh, you could see the mark of army boot, and on the right kidney and on the right thigh - I don't know exactly - he again had two prints of those boots, one above the other. His one ear was cut. Because he had to write a statement that he had not been selling weapons, that he was in agreement with the Serb Krajina, that he had not participated in any attack organised against Serb Krajina. He wrote that in Latin alphabet; however, they forced him to eat that sheet of paper and then forced him to write it in Cyrillic. Then he wrote it in Cyrillic. Yes, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement, you also describe what he had to do with the piece of paper on which he was writing in Latin script. Do you still remember what it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes. He had to eat it. I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I want to direct your attention to the date of 25th of June, 1992, and you mentioned in your statement that the village of Kotor was attacked. Do you know who attacked the village of Kotor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: The village of Kotor was attacked by Serb Specials and troops, and they also wore army uniforms and they expelled people from the village of Kotor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it all, because I live nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to redact this or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stated that you were able to observe it. Can you please elaborate on this, what you were able to see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: I could see fire being opened on the village of Kotor, because at my house, there was a machine-gun out there on the pitch, and there were mortars. And they -- and I saw them expel people across the bridge towards Kotor Varos, towards the hospital. There were some 50 men. Later on I heard that they had taken children to the school, to the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see who accompanied or escorted these men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: My husband and I were outside, and he saw -- and I saw too, people, four men, and I also saw a number of Serb Specials and uniformed men. They headed towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to hear anything unusual from the direction of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I heard bursts of fire and individual shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, did your husband recognise any of the soldiers who escorted these men towards the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: He took those four men from Kotor, because in 1991 when the war in Croatia started, they opened fire on the Catholic church. And he told me they had fired on the church. They will come to get me now and we won't fare well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did anyone come that day to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: They came sometime around half past 4.00, or perhaps 5.00. I'm not sure. Between 4.00 and 5.00. And they took both of us out of the house and my husband said: What do you want from me? I haven't done anything to you. I spent five days in a prison. Let me live. I'll do whatever you tell me to. And they said: We are policemen to you. We are your God. We want you. And they took both of us. Since I was barefoot, I asked one of them, with the long black hair, if I could go back and put slippers or shoes or something on. And he told me to go back, and I went back, and I started. And then he said: You have children. You can stay at home. So that I knew ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after this, did you go to the police station at some stage to find out what happened to your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes. I immediately went to the police station, but there was a curfew and I could not move about. We were allowed to move around only between 9.00 and 11.00. But I went to look for Dubocanin, and he said that one could look for him at any time, if need be. But he didn't come immediately. He came half an hour later. And I told him that men from Borce had taken him away, and he said that he would go after them. And after that, I went to the police station again to look for him, and in the morning, and he said: I'm sorry. Take care of the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, I will go back to the attack on Kotor. Do you know which ethnicity prevailed in that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: In that village, Muslims were a majority, and there were a few Croats. Perhaps two or three Serb houses, but they were all new.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned that that day, on 25th of June, you also saw a tractor. Can you describe, please, what exactly you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes. After that, after I had come back from the police station, I got into my flat. I looked through the windows. I looked outside and I saw a tractor covered with tarpaulin. And there were columns on two sides of it with a trailer. The tractor was -- and blood was oozing on two sides. It was around 6.00 or half past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: From your statement, we know that you left the Kotor Varos municipality on about 22nd August 1992, and now I would like to talk to you briefly about events or things which happened between the time of 11 of June and the time of your departure. You already mentioned that you saw this attack on the village of Kotor. Were you able to see from your apartment, or from somewhere else, any other incidents of attacks on other villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: No. Oh, I saw the village of Vecici attacked, but they were flying and bombing the village of Vecici. And on the 24th of June, I saw women and children in the village of Bilice being expelled towards Kotor Varos, towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement is written that on 24th of July, 1992, the village of Bilice was attacked. Today you said 24th of June. Is June the right month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: June, June. Not July. The 24th of June. Oh, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You already mentioned that there was a curfew. I would like to show to the witness a few documents and ask her to comment on them. The first one is Exhibit P2158. All these documents are from the Kotor Varos binder. Just to speed up the process, I made extra copies. I want witness to have a look on the page 00417168, because it is legible copy, unlike the following one. And we can see that it is decision -- we can place it on the ELMO. And it says: "Decision permitting citizens freedom of movement in the town from 9.00 to 11.00 hours." And it is decision of Kotor Varos municipality Crisis Staff, dated 15 of June, 1992. Do you remember this decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't, but I know that after -- when my husband came out of the police station, we went for a walk between 9.00 and 11.00. But they would inform us all over the town with a microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: What we had to do and how we could walk. But if you want me to remember when that was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, but you remember that there was this -- the freedom of moving between 9.00 and 11.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes. That I know. And I remember it well, because since my children were not with me, I had to go and get them. And I couldn't do it. They were staying with their grandparents. And between 9.00 and 11.00 I had to go to the Crisis Staff to apply for a permit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We'll talk about this in a moment. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with this document, and I would like to show the witness another one, which is P2180.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in a moment I will play you a video showing some news, but this document is extract from the minutes of the 44th session of the Crisis Staff held on 28th of June, 1992. And under item 1, the second paragraph, it says: "It was agreed that a public announcement should be made calling upon the population to report to the newly established authorities any extremist groups in their villages so they can be caught and destroyed." Do you remember any such or similar announcement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to play a video. I hope we will be able to play this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, but something happened with my monitor for sure. I mean, --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Something happened on my monitor on the video mode. Yes, it's okay: Video evidence now -- anyway, let's get the video and see whether we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For the interpreters, we are -- Exhibit P510. And for the interpreters, I am referring to the English translation, which is page 00917437, starting "Banja Luka television announcer." So if we could hear simultaneously as we go. And please listen to what -- and have a look on your monitor and tell us when we finish whether you saw this announcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: BANJA LUKA TELEVISION ANNOUNCER: -- expel the individuals who had arrived in our villages because your villages could be up in flames because of them. We are in particular calling upon the Muslim people not to be deceived by Croat extremists who push Muslims in front of them to kill Serbs. You must understand that the Croat -- Croatian policy uses Muslims for their own purposes. So Muslims go back to your homes, hand over your weapons, and forget about the extremists who wish no well to you or your children. To all those who return their weapons, we guarantee absolute safety of their property and person. This is what the Crisis Staff of Kotor Varos says in its announcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We can stop it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this news on TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were these announcements broadcast on a regular basis or was it only on one occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: This was broadcast frequently. I was horrified by it, because I know that other people did not organise anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I want to play another part from this video, and again, if you could tell us, after we will see it, whether you remember seeing this shot in the year 1992 or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: REPORTER: Could you please reply. Mr. Brdjanin, could you please tell us why you arrived and what is your assessment of the latest developments in the municipality. RADOSLAV BRDJANIN: My obligation as president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region is to visit all fronts. I must admit that most of the time I was in the corridor leading to Serbia. But simply, my visit, the reason for my coming here is that every Monday I must inform the presidents of Crisis Staffs about the political situation in this area. We must clean up our area, which unquestionably includes Kotor Varos and Jajce, and the most important battle which is under way and which I attended yesterday is the break through to Serbia. Simply, we can see for ourselves that there can be no more negotiations with those waging war against us. Those who took up arms must be defeated, hand them over, and total Serb authority must rule here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember seeing this shot on TV, either in -- not either. In 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you watch -- was it on Banja Luka television or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes, TV Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you watch it regularly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: I didn't follow it regularly, but I did as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I want to change a little bit the subject and ask you about your departure. And again, I want to show the witness a few documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, these documents, if I think you're referring to the ones I have in front of me, bear her name?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. When we get to that, please do remind me so that we into closed session or private session or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The first document is Exhibit 2182.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it says: "All those willing to move out of Kotor Varos are to make a statement at the lower court, leaving the immovable property to the social and political community." My first question is: Were there any announcements broadcast or transmitted in some other way, which would state that non-Serb or any population can leave the municipality of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes, there were announcements over the radio and television, but also every afternoon at 4.00 p.m. there was a vehicle with a microphone, and it would state when the convoy was leaving, when we can pack, where we can register, where we can report to, and that we could leave Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And as this document states that you had to go to make a statement at the lower court. Was it the only authority you have to visit or did you have to obtain some other permissions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: It wasn't the only statement that I had to give. I had to go to the Crisis Staff, to the SUP, to get a permit, also to pay 200 German marks. And I think I gave you those two certificates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. We will deal with them in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to show the witness another document. It is Exhibit P2218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the English version on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this document which you probably didn't see states that one Lubija Gavric [phoen] is to compile and forward to the presidency a detailed report on the resettlement of population, including the following data: "The number of convoys moved out so far, the number of persons who have moved out, and the conditions under which they moved out. Financial report with updated information on receipts, and expenditures, and other relevant information." As we already heard, you left on 22nd or 23rd of August. But were -- 1992. But were there any convoys before this date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: There were a couple of convoys. I don't know exactly how many. I know only when my sister-in-law went out. I went to town to see her off with the children, and this was something that was very difficult for me, because then I remained there alone. My parents were in the village. The children were not with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That day you went to see your sister-in-law, do you still remember approximately how many people were leaving that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: I don't remember. I just said goodbye to her and I left, because it was still curfew. I went with a Serb woman. She was allowed to move around.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us at least how many buses or trucks you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention to that. I just know how many there were when I left, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you remember whether there was at least more than one bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: There were several. There were a lot of people. There were more than two or three hundred people there. They were all waiting in line to register, and the line stretched from the municipality building to the -- to one of the cafes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us what ethnicity were people who were leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: All those people were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness Exhibit P2192.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had to go to the offices of the Crisis Staff to get some permissions. Did you know --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT71
utterances.text: Yes. Since my children were up in Obodnik, I had to go and collect them. And since we didn't have a car, we had nothing, I didn't know how to go there. I went to the Crisis Staff four times to ask for a receipt, and this had to be between 9.00 and 11.00, and I was not able to get this receipt, because Mr. Djekanovic wasn't there or they didn't let me in. Once Mr. Komljenovic came by. He used to go to school with me. And he asked me what I wanted there, and I told him that I wanted to bring my children. He said: Where are the children? I said: They're in Obodnik. And then he said: What do you need? And I said: I needed a certificate, a receipt, in order to be able to move around. And then he said: Okay and he issued this permit. He went inside, gave me the permit, and then I went to collect the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
